speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As with this House, I am concerned about the disruption.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our imperative must be to get to the bottom of the matter, take follow-up actions and prevent similar incidences from recurring.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) has, therefore, investigated the incident thoroughly, with inputs from operator SMRT and the equipment supplier Alstom.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They identified what went wrong and have started to address the gaps and shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On 28 October, that is, last month, LTA issued a detailed media statement and its full investigation report.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Together with SMRT and Alstom, they held a joint media briefing the same day to explain the cause of the incident, the follow up actions and answered many questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Their findings, including answers to many of the questions posed by Members, were widely covered in the media.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, there was a 22kV power cable fault in the electrical zone between Tuas Link and Tuas West Road stations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This would not have caused a disruption if the circuit breaker, which is a protection feature of the system, had kicked in and isolated the affected electrical zone because, once isolated, the power can flow and service can continue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But then a second fault occurred, in that the circuit breaker at Tuas West Road station, close to where the faulty cable was, malfunctioned.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It was later found out that the trip coil, which is a component of the circuit breaker, was faulty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A secondary protection mechanism at the sector level did kick in and then isolated the fault.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that cut off power supply across large sections of the North-South and East-West Lines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At that point, the Operations Control Centre then made a mistake and did not isolate the fault before drawing power from the Buona Vista Intake substation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the Buona Vista Intake substation also supplies power to the Circle Line, this, in turn, affected train services along parts of the Circle Line.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members have asked: why was the power cable faulty?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why did the primary circuit breaker, which is the first level of protection, not work?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why did the Operations Control Centre not remotely isolate the fault before powering up?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: LTA, SMRT and Alstom have given their explanations during the media briefing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The reasons for the component failures are still unknown.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The faulty power cable and the circuit breaker have been sent for forensic examination by the original equipment manufacturer, to ascertain the reasons for failure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What we do know is that there have been four power cable failures along the Tuas West Extension since 2018.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: LTA and SMRT had earlier expressed their concerns to Alstom, the supplier, who was forthcoming and had already agreed much earlier to replace some of the cables.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, work was on track to start in the later part of October.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is quite a major undertaking and will be completed progressively by the end of next year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The cables will take time to procure and arrive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the right time, LTA will schedule early closures and late openings on weekends or full Sunday closures for limited periods in 2021 to facilitate the cable replacement works.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will announce these plans in due course.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: LTA will implement weekend early closures to facilitate the replacement exercise and we seek commuters' understanding for the inconvenience caused.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is in addition to visual inspections of the trip coils once every 10 days, to ensure that they are in working order.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the Operations Control Centre not isolating the fault before drawing power from Buona Vista Intake substation, this was a human error.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members asked if there was a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in responding to such a situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are, in fact, many sets of SOPs to cater to different scenarios, but one thing we have learnt over the years is that every disruption is different and unique.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, besides being guided by SOPs, the engineers on duty will have to exercise judgement and make quick decisions during an emergency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have not been in their shoes and cannot imagine the challenges they are facing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But under the pressure of time and circumstances, the personnel involved, I believe, made an honest mistake.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have no doubt this has been a major lesson for them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They wished they had decided differently and they have much learning to share with their colleagues, so that such a mistake will not happen again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members also asked about evacuation and crowd control.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to assure Members that LTA, SMRT and the Home Team jointly conduct emergency preparedness exercises every year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SMRT staff also regularly get refreshed on their roles and responsibilities during a service disruption.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the evening of the disruption, the SOPs were promptly implemented.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: About 400 additional SMRT staff were immediately activated to both rectify the fault and help affected commuters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Safety of commuters is the top priority during service recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why detraining commuters is always a last resort because to have commuters walking along the track poses risk, especially for those who are elderly or handicapped.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, they need to be very carefully carried out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Operations Control Centre, therefore, has to balance the risk posed by detrainment against the discomfort and heightened anxiety of commuters in the stalled trains.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Train captains carried out the safety protocols, and station staff walked on the tracks to the trains to guide commuters to the nearest stations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Despite this, crowds built up around the MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is, unfortunately, inevitable in the event of a train disruption.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While there is understandably concern about overcrowding, given the current COVID-19 situation, it will not be practical to ensure physical distancing without further inconveniencing the affected commuters in such an unexpected situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The transport team simply has to do our best to prevent such incidents from happening in the first place and to rectify the incidents as quickly as possible should they occur.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Thankfully, on that evening, commuters were very cooperative.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They continued to wear their masks and minimised talking to each other, and I thank the commuters for their understanding and for doing their part under such trying circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the course of their investigations, our engineers learnt many useful lessons, to improve operations and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are also wider, non-engineering lessons, too, for policy makers and, I think, for this House as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, mass rapid transit systems are very complex.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Engineers who have worked on mass rapid transit systems and other systems, and have a basis for comparison, will very likely testify to that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Several fields of engineering converge to get a mass rapid transit system to work reliably to carry millions of commuters safely, for many hours throughout the day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given its complexity, when a major disruption occurs, the circumstances and causes are often unique.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That leads us to the second lesson – because of the nature of mass rapid transit systems, we should never be complacent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Always emphasise building up engineering and operational capabilities and experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Regularly review SOPs and conduct staff training to ensure processes are up to date and everyone in the team knows what to do when the need arises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, MOT, LTA, SMRT and SBST must work as one team.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the spirit of the One Transport Team.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the recent disruption, the morale of the teams on the ground has taken a hit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nobody wishes for an incident like this to happen, but when it did, we should not let it break our spirit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are honest and hardworking people who have toiled over the past few years to make our MRT system amongst the most reliable in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By believing in them and in ourselves, we can stand tall, be united again and press on with our work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, as a team, we take collective responsibility, not finger point, and we will do our best, close the gaps and address the shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Only then can we continue to fulfil our collective mission of serving commuters well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How did they evacuate these vulnerable commuters, especially from trains that were stuck above ground?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is one of the reasons, in consideration of elderly and wheelchair-bound commuters, that detrainment had to be a last resort.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Yes, there are risks, especially for this group of commuters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But when we have to, you cannot have wheelchairs on the tracks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But on the Circle Line, in the tunnels, you can have wheelchairs because there is a side platform that you can push the wheelchair on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, evacuation on the Circle Line is much faster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For viaducts, the North-South East-West Line, it is not as straightforward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Typically, even when evacuation and detrainment start, the rest of the passengers can walk but the elderly and those with mobility challenges will stay on the train until further manpower, including SCDF, arrives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If need be, we use stretchers to carry such passengers to the nearest station.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The stations are also equipped with what we call battery-powered motorised trolleys that we can use and deploy to ferry them to the nearest station.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Walking on the viaduct has its risks and we will always be very careful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But most importantly, is to prevent such incidents from happening.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first is in regard to Minister's answer earlier that it took 40 minutes before a detrainment decision was taken and thereafter the commuters got off the trains in separate moments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is, is there a specific SOP – because there could be rising anxiety within the trains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my question, I was asking about good ventilation for commuters within the train itself, especially if you are stuck in the train for an hour or more before eventually detrainment, typically, how long is the SOPs before a decision is made?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be a fine being made against SMRT for such incidents; not just SMRT, but other providers going forward, in the future, if such incidents happen?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I want to emphasise you are balancing two unpleasant things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One is being trapped in a train and I can imagine the discomfort and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whenever there is a disruption like that, the battery does kick in the train.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Within an hour, you then have to decide whether to do the other unpleasant thing which is detrainment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a 750 volts DC, third rail, and you are walking next to it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You got to make sure you disable it, double confirm, triple confirm, quadruple confirm because it is no joke walking next to a 750 volts third rail.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, like on that night, there could be inclement weather and then there was lightning risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once there is lightning risk, you should stop.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you are balancing between these two things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But typically, after half an hour, a decision should be made whether to do detrainment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this case, there was some hope that they could repower, but the repower went wrong and brought down CCL, or sections of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Not an easy task but the Operations Control Centre of SMRT has to make those decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think the decisions they made that night, in terms of detrainment, was correct.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On companies that could be taken to task, if the operator has made a big boo-boo, resulting in a big disruption, of course, some of these actions would have to be looked into and there is a disciplinary framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think in this case, the investigation report went up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think what is more important than meting out punishment, is the team able to come together, reflect upon what could be done better and take it upon themselves, take responsibility to say, "I can do things better".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And together, without finger-pointing, work together to better serve commuters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The mood can easily change and go wrong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When it becomes one of penalty and punishment, then the mood changes when everyone become defensive, everyone, to put it crudely, will cover their behinds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And after a while, you do not get the best outcome.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, as far as possible, there is a disciplinary structure and we will use it if we have to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as far as possible, I feel, hold the team together, be able to work together for the benefit of commuters – that is a lot more important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, beyond the suspension of the two staff, will LTA look into how the SMRT or indeed, both rail operators, can improve their work processes in future to prevent or mitigate against similar staff, human error in similar situations like this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, in respect of the proposed replacement cables by Alstom, whether LTA will require more stringent tests to be conducted on the replacement of the upper layer cables, to ensure that similar faults which were spotted on the current cables on the previous four occasions, as well as which caused 14 October disruption, will not be present in the future replacement cables.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think to put it in context, this set of components and equipment are not new.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not want to prejudge why the cable was faulty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is going through forensics and once the results come out, I am sure it will provide insights.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there is an SOP and there is an inspection regime for all cables and trip-coils throughout the system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the first question, I should I emphasise, suspension does not necessarily mean we are blaming the workers or they are being punished.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But in most operations involving live operations and in a place where there is a strong safety culture, suspensions are not uncommon.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is actually carried out, quite routinely, as a matter of professional conduct and safety protocol.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You will find that in the SAF, you find it in bus operations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You have a near-miss, or a side swipe of a bus, the captain might be suspended for a week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does not mean it is a punishment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, it is not their fault, or even running theme parks or manufacturing plants, process plants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is part and parcel of a professional conduct of an engineering company.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The purpose, depending on the circumstances, need not always be punishment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, it is really a matter of retraining, refresh what you have learnt, self-reflect and go back, you do better and share your learnings with your colleagues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think it is a good system to ensure that we keep on improving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The question specifically asked if there would be improvement in work processes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have mentioned, every time there is a major disruption, it is always unique.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SMRT has not encountered such a situation before where a cable fault, coupled with a trip-coil fault, resulting in a disruption.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But frankly, when it happens, you do not have time to go and refer to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has to be internalised into the experience and lessons learnt by all the operators, and by the engineers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think this incident provided a lot of lessons for them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just one supplementary question specific to the faulty cable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister mentioned that the cable is now being forensically examined as to the reason its failure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the earlier episodes of cable failure, was it a consistent reason as in there were not two or three different reasons so that the OEM could not identify why the cable is failing in the same way, or could this have been pre-empted to an extent if the earlier cable failures were all down to the same reason or same cause?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this year, there were two earlier failures, now this one.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the reasons for the failure has not been established which is why, given that what has happened, we should send it for forensic examination and understand the reason why.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, regardless of the reason, the cables would be replaced.
